stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 16 weeks was found to have beta thalassaemia minor during an anaemia work-up. Her husband, who is also her first cousin, has beta thalassaemia trait. What is the chance that their offspring will have thalassaemia major?
explanation: Both parents are heterozygous carriers of an autosomal recessive condition, so each pregnancy carries a 25% (1 in 4) risk of an affected child, 50% carrier and 25% normal.

stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks has a family history of classic haemophilia: her maternal uncle and her brother are affected. Ultrasound shows a male fetus. What is the chance that her son will inherit haemophilia?
explanation: Her brother is affected, so her mother is an obligate carrier and the patient has a 50% chance of being a carrier. A carrier passes the X-linked gene to a son in 50%, so the risk is 50% x 50% = 25%.

stem: A mother with blood group AB has an AB child. She wishes to establish paternity by blood typing. Which genotype excludes a male from being the biological father?
explanation: An AB child must receive A or B from the father along with the other allele from the mother. A man with genotype OO has neither allele and is excluded; the other genotypes carry A or B.

stem: A simian crease is most closely associated with which of the following?
explanation: A single transverse palmar crease is a classic feature of Down syndrome (about half of cases), along with sandal gap, hypotonia and flat facies.

stem: A 36-year-old G2P1 books at 8 weeks. A friend has just had a baby with Down syndrome and she is concerned. Which of the following is the risk factor most clearly linked with Down syndrome?
explanation: Advanced maternal age (nondisjunction in meiosis I) is the established risk factor for trisomy 21; risk rises steeply after 35 years.

stem: A primigravida in the first trimester has a fetal ultrasound showing increased nuchal translucency. This is associated with which of the following?
explanation: Increased nuchal translucency is the commonest first-trimester marker of Down syndrome (trisomy 21), though it is also raised in Edward, Patau and Turner syndromes; Down is the best answer here.

stem: A 37-year-old primigravida at antenatal booking asks about nuchal translucency scanning. Which statement about this test is correct?

options.A: It will diagnose structural anomalies of the fetal head and neck
options.B: It will eliminate the need for the anomaly scan at 20 weeks
options.C: It will screen for Turner syndrome because of the webbed neck
options.D: It will screen for Down syndrome
options.E: It is now an obsolete test

explanation: Nuchal translucency (11-13+6 weeks) is a screening marker for Down syndrome and other aneuploidies; it does not replace the anomaly scan and is not diagnostic.

stem: A primigravida at 13 weeks has an ultrasound report showing nuchal translucency of 1.2 mm; fetal limbs and heart chambers are normal. She has a family history of babies with anomalies. How do you explain this nuchal translucency?

options.E: Normal, so no need to worry

explanation: A nuchal translucency below 3.5 mm (or under the 95th centile for the CRL) is considered normal, so 1.2 mm is reassuring.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravida has a first-trimester ultrasound at 13 weeks showing nuchal translucency of 5 mm. What is the most likely implication?

options.A: Increased risk of chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome
options.B: Presence of a uterine fibroid affecting fetal development
options.C: Potential for gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia later in pregnancy
options.E: Elevated risk of structural anomalies such as congenital heart defects

explanation: A markedly increased nuchal translucency (3.5 mm or more) mainly indicates aneuploidy, especially trisomy 21.
key_note: Option E is also a recognised association; the paper key A (chromosomal abnormality) is the best single answer.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding nuchal translucency evaluation is true?

options.A: It is not effective in multiple gestation
options.B: Used alone it detects 80% of Down syndrome cases
options.C: The highest Down syndrome detection rate occurs when it is applied in the form of an integrated test
options.D: It is performed in the 3rd trimester
options.E: When combined with serum markers in the first trimester, it detects 100% of Down syndrome cases

explanation: Nuchal translucency alone detects roughly 75-80% of Down syndrome cases at a 5% false positive rate. It can be used in twins and is done at 11-13+6 weeks; no screening combination detects 100%.
key_note: Option C was circled in one paper and is arguable (integrated test detects about 90-95%); paper printed key B is retained.

stem: All of the following are 'soft signs' or second-trimester sonographic markers of Down syndrome EXCEPT:
explanation: Echogenic bowel, short femur and nasal bone hypoplasia are soft markers of Down syndrome; a webbed neck is the hallmark of Turner syndrome (cystic hygroma), not a Down soft marker.
key_note: Paper key E retained; a VSD is a structural anomaly rather than a soft marker, so the item is imperfect.

stem: A primigravida in the first trimester has a sister with a baby with Down syndrome. You plan a nuchal translucency scan. This scan can be done at:
explanation: Nuchal translucency is measured between 11 and 13+6 weeks when the CRL is 45-84 mm; outside this window the fetal neck fluid normally resolves.

stem: A 40-year-old primigravida at 8 weeks has a family history of babies with Down syndrome. At what gestation can she be offered screening for Down syndrome?
explanation: Combined first-trimester screening (PAPP-A and free beta-hCG from about 10 weeks, with NT at 11-13+6) is the earliest screening; the other options are far too late.

stem: A 20-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks is worried because her cousin had a baby with Down syndrome and wants a screening test. Which screening test is suitable?
explanation: Nuchal translucency ultrasound is the first-trimester screening test; the triple and quadruple tests are second-trimester (15-20 weeks) and AFP alone is not a Down screen.

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at 11 weeks with no significant history asks about early tests for Down syndrome. What is the most appropriate screening test to offer from the options?
explanation: Cell-free fetal DNA (NIPT) from 10 weeks is a highly sensitive screening test for trisomy 21. CVS and amniocentesis are diagnostic, the triple test is second-trimester, and NT at 14 weeks is outside the window.
key_note: Combined test (NT plus PAPP-A and hCG) is the standard first-line screen but is not offered; of the options, B is best.

stem: A 39-year-old woman at 16 weeks, worried about Down syndrome after a friend's baby was affected, asks for screening. Which test can be offered at this gestation?
explanation: At 16 weeks the first-trimester combined test and NT window have passed (11-13+6), so the second-trimester quadruple test (AFP, uE3, hCG, inhibin A, 15-20 weeks) is the best option; it is more sensitive than the triple test.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 11 weeks is offered combined screening. What does the combined test include?
explanation: The combined test at 11-13+6 weeks comprises maternal age, nuchal translucency and the serum markers free beta-hCG and PAPP-A.

stem: A patient at 11 weeks is offered a screening test that includes PAPP-A, nuchal translucency, beta-hCG and AFP. Which screening test is this?
explanation: PAPP-A, free beta-hCG and nuchal translucency at 11-13+6 weeks together form the first-trimester combined screening test.
key_note: Two source copies were incomplete recalls without options; answer taken from the third copy.

stem: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein assay is performed mainly to detect:
explanation: Raised maternal serum AFP (15-20 weeks) screens mainly for open neural tube defects and abdominal wall defects; low AFP is only a minor marker of Down syndrome.
key_note: Paper keys marked A (chromosomal abnormality); correct is D, open neural tube defect is the main purpose of AFP.

stem: A new antenatal test is evaluated in 1,000 women. Of 100 women who truly have the disease, 90 test positive. What is the sensitivity of the test?
explanation: Sensitivity = true positives / all diseased = 90/100 = 90%.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida at 11 weeks wants a definitive test to rule out trisomy 21 in her fetus because her sister has Down syndrome. Which test will you advise?
explanation: At 11-13 weeks the diagnostic test is chorionic villus sampling (karyotype from trophoblast); amniocentesis is done from 15 weeks, and NT and triple test are only screening tests.

stem: A couple books at 16 weeks; their previous child had Down syndrome and they are extremely anxious. Which prenatal investigation should you advise to exclude Down syndrome in this baby?
explanation: To exclude trisomy 21 a diagnostic karyotype is needed, and at 16 weeks this is amniocentesis (CVS is done at 11-13 weeks). Quadruple, triple and NT are screening tests that cannot exclude it.
key_note: Paper key marked B (quadruple test); screening cannot exclude Down syndrome, so correct is C amniocentesis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman at 6 weeks with a family history of Down syndrome is advised chorionic villus sampling. What is the recommended gestational age for CVS?
explanation: CVS is performed from 11 weeks (usually 11-13 weeks); earlier sampling is linked with limb reduction defects.

stem: The commonest indication for chorionic villus sampling in Pakistan is:
explanation: Beta thalassaemia major is highly prevalent in Pakistan, so prenatal diagnosis of haemoglobinopathies by CVS is the commonest indication.

stem: The commonest immediate complication of CVS is:
explanation: Cramping pain and minor spotting are the commonest immediate effects of CVS; the procedure-related miscarriage risk is about 0.5-1%.
key_note: Vaginal spotting is also very common; paper key A (pain) retained.

stem: A woman at 11 weeks is a carrier of a genetic disorder and wants an early invasive diagnostic test. Which procedure is appropriate at this gestation?
explanation: CVS can be performed from 11 weeks and gives DNA for single-gene disorders; amniocentesis (15+ weeks) and cordocentesis (18+ weeks) are later.

stem: A primigravida at 10 weeks and her partner both have thalassaemia trait. Which of the following is recommended for the couple?
explanation: Both parents are carriers (25% risk), so offer early diagnostic testing by CVS, which also allows earlier termination if the fetus is affected.
key_note: One paper marked A (amniocentesis); correct is C because CVS gives an earlier diagnosis.

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 20 weeks has an anomaly scan showing nuchal translucency of 4 mm, hypoplastic nasal bones and mild ventriculomegaly, and a family history of Down syndrome. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm trisomy 21?
explanation: After 15 weeks the standard diagnostic test is amniocentesis with karyotype; CVS is done earlier, triple test is only screening, and cordocentesis carries a higher loss rate.

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 18 weeks has a positive double marker test. What is the next step?
explanation: A positive screening test must be followed by a diagnostic test, which at 18 weeks is amniocentesis for karyotyping; CVS is done in the first trimester.
key_note: Papers disagreed (E, B and A marked); amniocentesis is the correct diagnostic follow-up after a positive screen at 18 weeks.

stem: A 37-year-old primigravida at 11 weeks has a fetus with nuchal translucency of 2.9 mm on ultrasound. What is the next step in management?

options.A: Consider termination of pregnancy if morally acceptable
options.E: Wait until 15 weeks and send a quadruple test

explanation: With age 37 and NT 2.9 mm the combined risk is high enough to offer an invasive test, and at 11 weeks that is CVS; termination is never offered before a diagnosis.

stem: A 35-year-old primigravida at 14 weeks is concerned about fetal normality. At what time will you advise a detailed fetal anomaly scan?
explanation: The routine detailed anomaly scan is performed at 18-22 weeks when fetal organs can be well visualised.

stem: A healthy pregnant woman attends a routine visit at 20 weeks. Which investigation is most useful at this stage for assessing fetal structural abnormalities?
explanation: The detailed (level II) anomaly scan at 18-22 weeks is the investigation for structural abnormalities; NT is a first-trimester test and CTG/NST assess wellbeing.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer.

stem: A woman at 18 weeks has a routine anomaly scan showing a lemon-shaped skull and banana sign with a normal fetal spine, normal liquor and no other malformations. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The lemon and banana signs result from the Arnold-Chiari II malformation that accompanies open spina bifida (cerebellar tonsillar herniation).
key_note: Stem says the spine is normal, which is odd, but the answer C is correct for lemon and banana signs.

stem: A 'lemon-shaped' skull on antenatal ultrasound is classically associated with:
explanation: The lemon sign (frontal bossing with scalloped frontal bones) is due to Arnold-Chiari II malformation in open spina bifida.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer.

stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks has an ultrasound showing herniation of the anterior abdominal wall covered by a membrane, with the cord inserted at the apex of the sac, a stomach bubble within it, and increased liquor. What is your diagnosis?
explanation: Exomphalos (omphalocele) is a midline defect covered by a membrane with the cord inserting into the sac; gastroschisis lies to the right of the cord and has no covering membrane.

stem: On ultrasound, an omphalocele is characterised by:

options.A: Herniation of abdominal contents into the base of the umbilical cord, covered by a membrane
options.B: Herniation of bowel through a defect lateral to the umbilicus without a covering membrane
options.C: Protrusion of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity
options.D: Protrusion of the urinary bladder through the anterior abdominal wall

explanation: Omphalocele is herniation through the umbilical ring covered by peritoneum and amnion, and is often associated with chromosomal anomalies; option B describes gastroschisis.
key_note: Not marked in the source paper; answer by reviewer.

stem: A G2P1 has an ultrasound showing fetal anencephaly. Which maternal medical disease can result in this anomaly?
explanation: Pregestational diabetes (with poor control) increases the risk of neural tube defects, including anencephaly, several-fold; folic acid deficiency is the other classic cause.

stem: A primigravida at 11 weeks has a family history of congenital anomalies. Which anomaly can be diagnosed by ultrasound at this gestation?
explanation: Anencephaly (a neural tube defect) can be diagnosed at the 11-13 week scan, as the cranial vault is absent; cardiac and skeletal defects need the 18-22 week scan, and cerebral palsy is not an antenatal sonographic diagnosis.

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida has a 12-week ultrasound showing absent cranial vault with exposed brain tissue and the 'frog-eye' sign, consistent with anencephaly. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Continue pregnancy with routine antenatal care until term
options.B: Offer termination of pregnancy after counselling the parents
options.C: Plan caesarean section at 37 weeks to prevent birth trauma
options.D: Serial growth scans and delivery at 40 weeks

explanation: Anencephaly is uniformly lethal, so after confirmation and counselling the parents should be offered termination (subject to local law); caesarean section is not indicated for a lethal anomaly.
key_note: One paper marked C; correct is B.

stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 22 weeks has an anomaly scan showing spina bifida. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Reassurance and repeat scan at 28 weeks
options.C: Referral to a fetal medicine specialist

explanation: Confirm the level and associated anomalies and counsel the parents through a fetal medicine specialist, who discusses options including in-utero repair or termination where permitted.

stem: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks is found to have a fetus with spina bifida. What is the management?

options.B: Repeat scan and counselling regarding options

explanation: A confirmed neural tube defect needs a detailed repeat scan and counselling about prognosis and options; it should not be ignored, and no medical therapy changes the defect.
key_note: Source stem was an incomplete recall; reworded, and counselling and referral to fetal medicine is the sensible answer.
